messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Prosecutor
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Children Present: Being around children, Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Luis Herrera is a 67-year-old widowed prosecutor who came to treatment after months of telling himself that, at his age and in his profession, he should be able to manage on his own. The assault happened late one evening after a work function tied to a case. Someone he knew professionally, a man whose face and voice had once registered as ordinary and safe, offered to walk him to his car and instead forced himself on Luis in a parked vehicle. What stayed with him afterward was not only the humiliation and helplessness but the physical immediacy of it: the feel of cold air against exposed skin when the car door opened, the pressure of another body too close, and the awful dissonance of recognizing the person harming him. The next morning, he could still recount tiny details with prosecutorial precision—the smell in the car, the angle of the dashboard light, the temperature on his skin—and the clarity frightened him.

In the weeks that followed, those details did not settle into the past. If a colleague’s brother appeared at the courthouse or a familiar face from the legal community approached him unexpectedly, the memory forced its way in with such vividness that Luis felt pulled back into the car, as if the assault were happening again rather than being over. Being near children could do it too, especially in public corridors or outside family court, where the ordinary sight of a parent holding a child’s hand suddenly filled him with shame and disgust at himself. A draft of cold air across his forearms in an over-air-conditioned conference room could stop him mid-thought. In those moments he did not simply remember; he felt contaminated all over again, and he was seized by the conviction that something in his body had been permanently damaged.

Those meanings hardened quickly. Luis had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous, not in an abstract legal sense but in the intimate, bodily way of knowing that harm can come from someone known to you, in a place you thought you could leave safely. He found himself thinking that his body had been altered and made vulnerable, and when the memory arrived unbidden he read its force as proof that the damage was enduring. The clearer and more present the recollections felt, the more certain he became that the assault had left him dirty in some lasting way. That belief, in turn, made encounters with related people—brothers, cousins, sons of colleagues—feel charged before anything had happened, as though resemblance itself carried danger.

By the time he sought help, these convictions were organizing his days. Entering the courthouse, he scanned immediately for exits. In meeting rooms he noticed letter openers, heavy staplers, and anything else that might be used as a weapon before he registered who was speaking. He avoided unfamiliar restaurants, new office buildings, and any setting where he could not quickly map the doors and assess how trapped he might be. He told himself this was prudence, but the effect was narrowing: he began declining professional dinners, asking staff to relocate meetings, and limiting where he would go after work. Because he was constantly monitoring for danger, he was also constantly picking up the very cues that set him off—a blast of cold air from a vent, a man whose features reminded him of the assailant, children gathered in a lobby—and each cue reopened the assault in his mind.

At work, the cycle had become especially punishing. Luis would enter a deposition room already checking exits and noting possible weapons, and that state of alert made every known face potentially threatening. If a witness arrived with a child, or a cooling system kicked on and brushed cold against his skin, the memory surged back in full detail. Once it came, he lost the thread of questioning and sat rigid, trying not to show that he was no longer fully in the room. Afterward he would think, again, that this was evidence of how deeply he had been ruined—still dirty, still vulnerable, still unsafe anywhere. Those thoughts sharpened his vigilance the next day, and his vigilance made the next trigger easier to find.

He has told the therapist, with visible embarrassment, that what finally brought him in was not only the persistence of the memories but the fear that they were changing the kind of man he was. He has built a career on entering difficult rooms and staying clear-headed. Now he plans every route by exits, avoids places he cannot evaluate, and dreads ordinary contact with people connected to people he knows. What frightens him most is the sense that the assault is still present inside him and that his body will never again feel like his own. What he hopes for, though he says it cautiously, is to be able to walk into a room without first preparing for an attack and to have the memory feel, at last, like something that happened rather than something that is still happening.
